line01-01.png.text: In this video, I'm going to show you how I build a feature with Devin when I want to stay hands-on: working in the IDE and the terminal next to the agents, instead of handing the whole task off.

line02-01.png.text: I'll use Devin Desktop and the Devin CLI. Local agents, cloud agents, and other agents like Codex and OpenCode all run here, in one app, with one session list.

line03-01.png.text: Setup is short. First, I connect GitHub to my Devin organization.

line04-01.png.text: Then Devin indexes my repositories in DeepWiki. These are the four repos for an insurance claims app: the Java claims service, the customer web portal, an adjuster desktop app, and an iOS app.

line05-01.png.text: DeepWiki gives me, and the agent, an architecture view of each repo. This is the claims service, generated from the code.

line06-01.png.text: In Desktop I open the portal and the service in one workspace. DeepWiki is right here in the IDE too.

line07-01.png.text: Here's my first task. It's a GitHub issue: let customers upload photos and documents to an open claim. Two sentences, no acceptance criteria.

line08-01.png.text: I pick Devin Local as the agent and switch to Plan mode, so it plans before it writes any code.

line09-01.png.text: For the model I pick Fusion, which pairs a frontier model with a faster one to keep the cost down.

line10-01.png.text: I ask it to plan this issue across the service and the portal, with acceptance criteria and a task list that shows what can run in parallel.

line11-01.png.text: Before it writes the plan, it asks me questions: which statuses count as open, where files are stored, which file types and limits. I answer them.

line12-01.png.text: Now I have a spec. It has the context it found in both repos, the decisions we made, and twelve acceptance criteria. Each one is testable: status codes, ownership, file types, limits.

line13-01.png.text: And here's the task list. There's a service track and a portal track, and the plan says which tasks depend on each other and which can run at the same time.

line14-01.png.text: The spec is just a file, so I can edit it. I tighten one criterion: list responses contain attachment metadata only.

line15-01.png.text: Nothing is built until I approve the plan.

line16-01.png.text: I approve it, but I scope this local session to the portal screen only. Other agents get the rest.

line17-01.png.text: For the service track, I open the Devin CLI in the claims service and point it at the same plan file.

line18-01.png.text: Then I type slash handoff and pick Ubuntu. The CLI packages my conversation, my branch, and my uncommitted changes, and a cloud Devin picks it up in its own VM. My environment comes with me.

line19-01.png.text: The cloud agent is building and testing the API while my laptop stays free.

line20-01.png.text: From Desktop I start a second cloud session for the release notes, so the docs are written alongside the code.

line21-01.png.text: For the portal's proxy, I use Codex, running inside Devin Desktop through the Agent Client Protocol. It owns the proxy change and its tests.

line22-01.png.text: Here's the real work side by side: Codex's proxy change, and Devin Local's upload helpers.

line23-01.png.text: And this is what I mean by one surface. Devin Local, Codex, OpenCode, and my two cloud sessions are all in one session list, each with its status and pull request.

line24-01.png.text: The same cloud session is also in the Devin web app, with its PR.

line25-01.png.text: While Devin Local is working, I can queue a message. I edit it before it sends: keep it vanilla JavaScript, no new dependencies.

line26-01.png.text: I can also stop it outright.

line27-01.png.text: Then I give one correction: the button says "Upload file", with a hint for the allowed types and size. It picks up from where it was and makes the change.

line28-01.png.text: OpenCode wrote the customer help page, so I steer it the same way, and it updates the label.

line29-01.png.text: In the CLI, I can ask a quick side question with slash btw, without disrupting the main task. Here I ask where the proxy adds the customer headers, and it answers from the code.

line30-01.png.text: When the portal work is done, I hand it off from Desktop too. I pick Ubuntu again.

line31-01.png.text: The cloud agent receives my uncommitted changes, checks all eight files, runs the tests, and opens the pull request.

line32-01.png.text: Devin fits into my own harness. From Customizations, I open the plugin marketplace and install the official DeepWiki plugin.

line33-01.png.text: MCP servers are listed here. Plugins can bring their own.

line34-01.png.text: Hooks run my own scripts on agent events.

line35-01.png.text: And rules: both repos' AGENTS.md files are always on, so every agent follows the same conventions.

line36-01.png.text: I also want this upload checklist reused next time, so I ask Devin to turn it into a skill. It writes the SKILL.md.

line37-01.png.text: And now it shows up in Skills for any future session.

line38-01.png.text: For context, I generate a Codemap of the upload flow: from the portal, through the proxy, to the controller, the ownership check, validation, and storage. It's built from the code, and each step links back to it.

line39-01.png.text: Then I ask Devin Local to test it on my computer. It opens a browser and uploads a real PNG through the file picker.

line40-01.png.text: The file shows up on the open claim, with its size, and the request returned 201.

line41-01.png.text: The service pull request opens in Desktop's Review. Devin Review found no active bugs here.

line42-01.png.text: But the author noted a race at the twenty-file limit, so I ask Review chat to fix it. It drafts a lock and a concurrency test, and I commit it from here.

line43-01.png.text: Checks pass, and I merge the pull request from Desktop.

line44-01.png.text: On the portal PR, Review flags a critical issue: the demo proxy uses a fixed customer identity. That's a real finding, and it's the kind of thing I'd fix before production.

line45-01.png.text: Cost control starts with the model. Adaptive routes each request to the right model, and Fusion keeps frontier quality at a lower cost.

line46-01.png.text: In the CLI, slash session-stats shows the messages and tokens for the session.

line47-01.png.text: Desktop shows my daily and weekly usage.

line48-01.png.text: Admins control Desktop from organization settings: which models are allowed, and which MCP servers can be used.

line49-01.png.text: The ACP agent registry, and agent hooks for the whole organization.

line51-01.png.text: So that's assisted development with Devin: a spec I can read and edit, local, cloud, and ACP agents working in parallel, steering in real time, and review and merge, all from one app and one session list.
